quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-01.title: Sylow counting and growing normalizers
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-01.body:
**(a)** By Sylow's theorem, $|G:N|=n_7(G)=50$. Let $N\le H\le G$. Then $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_7(H)$ and $N_H(P)=N$, so $|H:N|=n_7(H)\equiv1\pmod7$. Also $|H:N|$ divides $|G:N|=50$. The divisors of $50$ are $1,2,5,10,25,50$, which are $\equiv1,2,5,3,4,1\pmod 7$. So $|H:N|\in\{1,50\}$, i.e. $H=N$ or $H=G$. As $|G:N|=50>1$, $N$ is a maximal subgroup.

**(b)** If $Q=1$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $Q\ne1$. Since $Q\trianglelefteq N$ is a Sylow $5$-subgroup of $N$, it is the unique one, so it contains every $5$-subgroup of $N$. Let $R\in\mathrm{Syl}_5(G)$ with $Q\subseteq R$. Then $R\cap N$ is a $5$-subgroup of $N$ containing $Q$, so $R\cap N=Q$. Since $5\mid50=|G:N|$, the $5$-part of $|G|$ exceeds that of $|N|$, so $Q\subsetneq R$.

In a finite $p$-group, a proper subgroup is properly contained in its normalizer ("normalizers grow"). Hence $N_R(Q)\supsetneq Q$. If $N_R(Q)\subseteq N$ we would have $N_R(Q)\subseteq R\cap N=Q$, a contradiction. So $N_R(Q)\not\subseteq N$, and $\langle N,N_R(Q)\rangle$ properly contains $N$; by (a) it equals $G$. Both $N$ and $N_R(Q)$ normalize $Q$, so $G$ normalizes $Q$, i.e. $Q\trianglelefteq G$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-02.title: Use the primary condition on $ab$
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-02.body:
Recall that a proper ideal $I$ is primary if $xy\in I$ and $x\notin I$ imply $y^n\in I$ for some $n\ge1$.

**(a)** Since $ab\in(ab)$ and $(ab)$ is primary, either $a\in(ab)$ or $b^n\in(ab)$ for some $n\ge1$. If $a\in(ab)$, write $a=abr$; then $a(1-br)=0$ with $a\neq0$ in a domain, so $br=1$ and $b$ is a unit — excluded. Hence $b^n\in(ab)\subseteq(a)$.

**(b)** Let $P\ne0$ be prime, fix $0\ne a\in P$, and let $b$ be any nonunit. As $(ab)$ is primary, part (a) gives $b^n\in(a)\subseteq P$ for some $n$, and since $P$ is prime, $b\in P$. So $P$ contains every nonunit. Conversely, $P$ is proper and so contains no unit. Hence $P$ equals the set of nonunits of $R$. This description does not depend on $P$, so any two nonzero primes coincide: $P$ is the unique nonzero prime ideal of $R$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-03.title: Roots are root-of-unity multiples of $\alpha$
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-03.body:
Let $a=\alpha^n\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $\alpha$ is a root of $x^n-a\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$, so $g\mid x^n-a$.

**(a)** The complex roots of $x^n-a$ are the numbers $\varepsilon\alpha$ with $\varepsilon^n=1$ (they are $n$ distinct roots, as $\alpha\ne0$). So the roots of $g$ are $\varepsilon_1\alpha,\dots,\varepsilon_m\alpha$ with $\varepsilon_i^n=1$, and
$$g(0)=(-1)^m\prod_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i\alpha=\delta\,\alpha^m,\qquad \delta=(-1)^m\textstyle\prod\varepsilon_i,$$
where $\delta$ is a root of unity. Since $g(0)\in\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha^m$ is real and nonzero, $\delta$ is real; the only real roots of unity are $\pm1$. So $g(0)=\pm\alpha^m$.

**(b)** By (a), $b:=\alpha^m=\pm g(0)\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $\alpha$ is a root of $x^m-b\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$, so $g\mid x^m-b$. Both are monic of degree $m$, hence $g(x)=x^m-b$.

**(c)** Write $n=qm+r$ with $0\le r<m$. Then $\alpha^r=\alpha^n/(\alpha^m)^q\in\mathbb{Q}$, say $\alpha^r=c$. If $r\ge1$, $\alpha$ is a root of $x^r-c$, so $g\mid x^r-c$, impossible as $0<r<m=\deg g$. Hence $r=0$ and $m\mid n$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-04.title: Minimal polynomial
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-04.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a basis with $Tv_i=\lambda_iv_i$, and let $\lambda\in K$. For $v=\sum k_iv_i$,
$$(\lambda I-T)v=\sum k_i(\lambda-\lambda_i)v_i,\qquad(\lambda I-T)^2v=\sum k_i(\lambda-\lambda_i)^2v_i.$$
By linear independence, each of these is $0$ iff $k_i=0$ for every $i$ with $\lambda_i\ne\lambda$. So both kernels equal the span of $\{v_i:\lambda_i=\lambda\}$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Since $K$ is algebraically closed, the minimal polynomial splits: $f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m(x-\lambda_i)$. Suppose it has a repeated root, say $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$, and put $g(x)=\prod_{i=3}^m(x-\lambda_i)$, so $f=(x-\lambda_1)^2g$. Then $(\lambda_1I-T)^2g(T)V=f(T)V=0$, so $g(T)V\subseteq\ker(\lambda_1I-T)^2=\ker(\lambda_1I-T)$. Hence $(T-\lambda_1I)g(T)=0$, so $T$ satisfies $(x-\lambda_1)g(x)$ of degree $m-1$, contradicting minimality. So $f$ has distinct roots.

Finally, a split minimal polynomial with distinct roots gives an eigenbasis: the polynomials $f_i=f/(x-\lambda_i)$ have no common root, so they are coprime and $1=\sum_if_ih_i$ for some $h_i\in K[x]$. Then every $v=\sum_if_i(T)h_i(T)v$, and $(T-\lambda_iI)f_i(T)h_i(T)v=f(T)h_i(T)v=0$, so $V=\sum_iE_{\lambda_i}$ is a sum of eigenspaces. The sum is direct (eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent), so the union of bases of the eigenspaces is a basis of eigenvectors. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-05.title: Graphs of homomorphisms
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1997f-05.body:
**(a)** The map $\phi\colon X\to V$, $\phi(x)=x-\theta(x)$, is an $R$-homomorphism, and $W_\theta=\phi(X)$, so $W_\theta$ is a submodule. For $x\in X$, $x=(x-\theta(x))+\theta(x)\in W_\theta+Y$; so $X\subseteq W_\theta+Y$ and $V=X+Y=W_\theta+Y$. If $w=x-\theta(x)\in W_\theta\cap Y$, then $x=w+\theta(x)\in X\cap Y=0$, so $x=0$ and $w=0$. Hence $V=W_\theta\dotplus Y$.

**(b)** Let $\pi\colon V=U\dotplus Y\to Y$ be the projection along $U$ (an $R$-homomorphism) and $\theta=\pi|_X\colon X\to Y$. For $x\in X$, write $x=u+\theta(x)$ with $u\in U$; then $x-\theta(x)=u\in U$, so $W_\theta\subseteq U$.

Conversely, let $u\in U$ and write $u=x-y$ with $x\in X$, $y\in Y$ (possible since $V=X\dotplus Y$). Then $x=u+y$ is the decomposition of $x$ in $U\dotplus Y$, so $\theta(x)=\pi(x)=y$ and $u=x-\theta(x)\in W_\theta$. Thus $U=W_\theta$. ∎
